name: Jamal Zhang

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time, Jamal. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers or government. Everything you tell me is confidential. Could you start by telling me a little about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Jamal, 27, and I do conveyancing at Whitlock and Sons, a four-lawyer firm in a market town. Conveyancing is the legal side of buying and selling houses: checking the deeds, the searches, the contracts, and moving the money on the day. I live on my own in a rented flat above a bakery on Church Street, so I wake up to the smell of bread, which is the best part of the morning.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And what does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: It's mostly files. I get a sale in, I order the searches from the council, I read the title documents, and I write to the other side's lawyer with a list of questions. The rest of the day is phone calls from buyers asking why it's taking so long. I don't use any AI, I do it the way Mrs Whitlock taught me, line by line with a ruler under the text. I'm not fast and I still miss things she catches, but I like that every file has an end.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say I told you so, a bit. Everyone at the Tuesday quiz kept saying I'd be replaced by a chatbot by now. I'd just say the old ways still work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: For me it's a relief about AI, but not about the job. The housing market round here has been slow for two years, and Whitlock and Sons is doing about half the sales it did. I've got maybe three weeks of rent in the bank, and the next conveyancing job is in the city, forty minutes on a bus that runs every hour.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going the way I am and try to get quicker, so Mrs Whitlock doesn't regret keeping me on. I'd cut back on eating out and the car I barely use, and put whatever I save aside. I wouldn't touch the AI tools even if they got a bit better.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but the normal kind. It's the same feeling I've had since the market slowed down. Every quiet week I look at the files on my desk and count them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens on a quiet week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have maybe six live files instead of fifteen, and I can hear Mr Whitlock on the phone to the bank about the overdraft. Last month he asked me to help with filing in the basement just to keep me busy. That's when I started counting files.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you sell the car?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd think about it. It's an old hatchback my dad gave me and it mostly sits outside the bakery. Selling my dad's hatchback would get me maybe a thousand, which is another month of rent, so yes, probably.

say: The **old ways** still work, and the AI hype was **overblown**.
I'd tease the **quiz crowd** who said a chatbot would replace me.
think: The **housing market** slump has halved the firm's sales, AI or not.
With **three weeks** of rent saved, the next job is a **forty-minute** bus ride.
do: Keep doing conveyancing by hand and try to **work faster**.
Cut back on eating out and possibly **sell the car**.
Keep **avoiding AI tools** even if they improved.
feel: **Worried** in a familiar way, **counting files** every quiet week.
S0.quote: Every quiet week I look at the files on my desk and count them.
fieldNote: His fear is the **slow housing market**, which already halved the firm's work.
He heard his boss talking to the bank about the **overdraft**, and it stuck with him.
He finds comfort in **old methods**, a ruler under the text, and avoids AI on principle.

steps.text: Keep checking deeds by hand and work on getting faster
Sell his dad's old hatchback for about a thousand
Put any savings from eating out into his bank account

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say people will still want a real person when they buy a house, it's the biggest thing they ever do. That's what I'd say at the quiz, anyway. I'd probably not say much online, I don't really post.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think conveyancing is exactly what the card means. Checking searches, writing standard questions, booking the money transfer: that's all on the list. The big online conveyancing firms already do it cheaper than us, and with AI they'll do it for nothing, and Whitlock and Sons will close.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay as long as the firm lasts, because I don't know what else I'd do. I'd ask Mrs Whitlock if I can shadow her on the wills and probate work, which feels more personal. I'd stop spending on anything that isn't rent and food.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Bad. Like the floor is tilting. I know I should be learning the new tools, and I just don't want to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You say you should learn the tools but don't want to. What stops you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think if I learn the AI tools, I'm helping build the thing that replaces me. And I'm not good with new systems, it took me four months to learn our case software. Mrs Whitlock doesn't use AI either, so I tell myself it's fine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if Whitlock and Sons closed? What would that day look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd probably go home, sit in the flat and listen to the bakery downstairs. Then I'd ring my mum, because she'd want to know before anyone else. I wouldn't have a plan, and that's what frightens me.

say: People still want a **real person** for the **biggest purchase** of their life.
I'd say it at the quiz, but I **wouldn't post** online.
think: **Conveyancing** is exactly the checking and booking the card describes.
Big **online firms** with AI will undercut Whitlock and Sons until it **closes**.
do: Stay at the firm for **as long as** it lasts.
Ask to **shadow** Mrs Whitlock on **wills and probate** work.
Cut spending to **rent and food** only.
feel: Guilty that he **should** learn the tools but doesn't want to.
S1.quote: If I learn the AI tools, I'm helping build the thing that replaces me.
fieldNote: He expects the **firm to close** and has no plan for that day.
His refusal to learn AI is part fear, part **principle**: not helping build his replacement.
He takes cover behind his boss, who also **doesn't use AI**.

steps.text: Stay at Whitlock and Sons for as long as it stays open
Ask Mrs Whitlock to let him shadow her on wills and probate
Cut all spending except rent and food

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what I'd say. Probably that it can't be that fast, somebody has to sign things. I'd be hoping I was right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I think I'd be done within a year. Everything I do is reading and writing documents, there's nothing a robot needs to come for. I don't have savings, I don't use the tools, and the only other law jobs are in the city doing the same work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't really have a plan, that's the truth. I'd keep turning up until they told me not to. Then I suppose I'd move back in with my parents in the next town and see if my dad's friend at the tyre place needs someone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Panicky. My chest goes tight even thinking about it. I'd feel like I'd wasted five years and a lot of my parents' money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the tyre place. How would you feel about that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It's hands-on, so it'd last until the robots, around 2031. My dad's friend Viktor has offered before, as a joke. A tyre place for three years is better than nothing, but I'd be starting again at 28 with nothing to show for my degree.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That I'm sorry. My parents paid my rent for the whole of law school, my mum cleaned offices at night to do it. Telling my mum the degree is worth nothing would be the worst conversation of my life.

say: It **can't be that fast**, because somebody has to sign things.
I'd be saying it mostly **hoping** I was right.
think: My job is **all documents**, so I'd be done within a year.
No **savings**, no AI skills, and other law jobs are the **same work**.
do: Keep turning up at the firm **until told** not to.
Move back in with his **parents** in the next town.
Ask his dad's friend Viktor for work at the **tyre place**.
feel: **Panicky**, with a **tight chest** just thinking about it.
Feels he'd have **wasted** five years and his parents' money.
S2.quote: Telling my mum the degree is worth nothing would be the worst conversation of my life.
fieldNote: He admits to having **no plan**, and the only fallback is his **parents' home**.
The three-year **robot gap** matters to him only through a possible **tyre-fitting** job.
**Guilt** toward his mother, who cleaned offices to pay his rent, is his deepest feeling.

steps.text: Keep turning up at Whitlock and Sons until told to stop
Give up the flat on Church Street and move back home
Lean on his parents for rent and food
Ask his dad's friend Viktor for work at the tyre place

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is a long time and the government will sort something out. That's what you say, isn't it. Everyone would be saying it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think I'd get a bit more time at the firm, but not enough to change what I'm good at. I'm slow to learn new things. Five years is long enough for Whitlock and Sons to fold, but not long enough for me to become something else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay put and try to save, maybe fifty a month, because I'm not going to get rich. I'd ask Mrs Whitlock to teach me probate, the sorting out of a person's affairs after they die, since families still want to talk to someone. If the firm closed before 2031, I'd look at the council's planning office, which is still paperwork but a steady wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still frightened, just slower. It's the same dread, spread out. Some days I'd forget, then a news story would bring it all back.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The council's planning office is thinking work too. Why there?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because it's the council, and the council never changes anything quickly. I know AI would get there too. I just think a council office would hang on to people longer than a small firm can.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You've said the government will sort something out. Do you believe it?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not really. I say it because it's easier than saying I'm scared. If I'm honest, I don't trust the government to sort out the bins on time, never mind this.

say: Five years is long, and the **government** will **sort something out**.
I'd repeat it because it's what **everyone** around me would be saying.
think: Five years is enough for the **firm to fold**, not for me to **change**.
I know I'm **slow** to learn new things.
do: Stay at the firm and save **fifty a month**.
Ask Mrs Whitlock to teach him **probate** work.
Look at the **council planning office** if the firm closes before 2031.
feel: **Frightened** but slower, the **same dread** spread out.
S3.quote: I don't trust the government to sort out the bins on time, never mind this.
fieldNote: His public line about the **government** isn't what he believes; he said so himself.
He chooses the **council** because it changes slowly, not because it's safe from AI.
Extra time doesn't change his **expected outcome**, only the pace of the **dread**.

steps.text: Save fifty a month while staying at Whitlock and Sons
Learn probate work from Mrs Whitlock
Apply to the council planning office if the firm closes

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fifth and last picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans."

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long way off and nobody really knows. I'd probably not talk about it much. People would say I should retrain, and I'd nod.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years means I could still be at Whitlock and Sons for a good while, maybe till Mrs Whitlock retires. But I'd be 37 doing a job that's about to vanish, with nothing else. That's almost worse, because I'd have had the time and not used it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going at the firm and finally learn probate properly over the first couple of years. I'd try to save a hundred a month and maybe get the car sold. I'd also look at an evening course in something hands-on, maybe plumbing, but I'd probably not sign up until I saw others doing it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy, but with a heavy bit underneath. It's like knowing a bill is coming but not when. I'd keep putting it off.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd probably not sign up. Why not?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I'm the kind of person who waits. I waited two years to change my phone. I know that's not how this works, but I know myself too.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If a younger cousin asked whether to study law, what would you say?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my cousin to do an apprenticeship, something with tools, and do law later if they still want it. Ten years from now I'd rather be fixing boilers than reading deeds nobody needs me to read.

say: **Ten years** is a long way off and **nobody knows**.
I'd **nod** when people told me to retrain, without committing.
think: I could stay at the firm until **Mrs Whitlock retires**.
Being 37 with **nothing else** and **unused time** would be almost worse.
do: Learn **probate** properly in the first couple of years.
Save a **hundred a month** and sell the car.
Look at an evening **plumbing course**, but likely wait to sign up.
feel: **Uneasy**, with a **heavy** feeling, like a bill coming with no date.
S4.quote: Ten years from now I'd rather be fixing boilers than reading deeds nobody needs me to read.
fieldNote: He knows he **waits** too long, and expects to do it here too.
He would steer a **cousin** toward an **apprenticeship**, not law.
Even with a decade, he still expects to **lose the job** with nothing ready.

steps.text: Learn probate from Mrs Whitlock over the next two years
Save a hundred a month and sell the old hatchback
Wait to see whether others take the evening plumbing course first

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The fast one, AGI by 2028. I don't have money, I don't have the skills for the new tools, and I don't have a plan. What would help is a proper paid apprenticeship for people my age, so I could train in something hands-on without losing the flat.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask what people are ashamed of. I'm a bit ashamed that I've had every warning and done nothing. That's probably the honest answer.

headlineQuote: I'm a bit ashamed that I've had every warning and done nothing.
portrait: Jamal is a **27-year-old** conveyancer at a **four-lawyer** firm, living alone above a bakery.
He works by hand with a **ruler** under the text and has **never used AI**.
The housing slump has already **halved** the firm's work, and he has **three weeks** of rent saved.
He moves from worried in AI Plateau to **panicked** in the two-year AGI picture, with **no plan**.
His fallbacks are his **parents' home**, a tyre place, or eventually a **plumbing** course he keeps postponing.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because he has no money, no AI skills and no plan.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid apprenticeship** for people his age in a **hands-on trade**, so he keeps his flat.
